claims.text: The target material is a single-phase, chemically disordered HEA in a uniform solid-solution state.
The proposed interatomic potential explicitly incorporates anharmonic phonon scattering.
The proposed interatomic potential explicitly incorporates local chemical disorder.
The proposed approach will predict low phonon thermal conductivities in single-phase HEAs more accurately than current semi-empirical methods.
Directly modeling the disorder-affected vibrational density of states explains the proposed improvement in thermal-conductivity prediction.
Phonon scattering dominates thermal transport at the moderate-to-high temperatures relevant to the proposed application.
Atomic-scale chemical disorder and anharmonic interactions modulate the vibrational density of states.
Atomic-scale chemical disorder and anharmonic interactions enhance phonon scattering.
Enhanced phonon scattering produces reduced phonon thermal conductivity.
Explicit treatment of disorder and anharmonicity links atomic structure to thermal conductivity more mechanistically than limited vibrational approximations.
Current comparison methods include empirical or CALPHAD-based extrapolations.
Current comparison methods lack detailed treatment of atomic-level disorder and anharmonic vibrational effects.
The proposed model will have a notably lower mean absolute error against measurements than current predictions.
The approach is applicable only to single-phase HEA regions in which disorder dominates vibrational properties.
The approach may fail in multiphase alloys or near order-disorder transitions because phase boundaries and secondary phases influence thermal transport.
The magnitude of the accuracy improvement may depend on the realized degree of anharmonicity and chemical disorder.
A measured phonon thermal conductivity differing from the prediction by more than 20% would falsify the hypothesis.
Observation of significant multiphase behavior in the benchmark material would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis explicitly excludes multiphase materials from its applicability domain, but the falsification rule treats significant multiphase behavior in the test specimen as falsifying the model. Such behavior would instead make the specimen an invalid out-of-domain benchmark.
